query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A nanocrystalline, refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coating, such as a CuMoTaWV film, when applied to a Cu matrix will form a well‐adhered, wear‐resistant surface. Its ultrafine grain structure and high hardness will significantly reduce wear by impeding plastic deformation and abrasive mechanisms, while its improved surface smoothness (after annealing) promotes strong adhesion at the coating/substrate interface.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional Cu matrix that exhibits relatively low wear resistance and moderate surface adhesion characteristics.
generation.intervention: Deposit a nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV HEA film onto the Cu matrix using a deposition technique (e.g., DC-magnetron sputtering) followed by a low-temperature annealing (e.g., 300 °C) to improve adhesion.
generation.conditions: Testing under reciprocating wear conditions at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures (up to ~300 °C) under specified sliding loads.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained, nanocrystalline HEA coating (with average grain sizes on the order of 18 nm) that has a reduced surface roughness after annealing.
generation.mechanism: The improved wear resistance stems from solid solution and grain-boundary strengthening that minimizes plastic deformation and abrasion. The nanocrystalline structure promotes mechanical interlocking with the Cu substrate. Simultaneously, the refined surface achieved after annealing reduces roughness and enhances chemical/mechanical bonding at the interface.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA-coated Cu matrix will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction, a reduced wear rate, and improved adhesion compared to uncoated Cu, thereby enhancing the overall surface protection in wear-critical applications.
generation.baseline: Uncoated Cu matrix surfaces show higher wear rates and inferior resistance under repeated sliding and abrasive conditions.
generation.boundary: This performance improvement is expected to hold under moderate operating temperatures and loads; under extreme thermal conditions or very high mechanical loads, differences in thermal expansion or additional stress factors may influence adhesion and wear behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in wear rate and adhesion strength is uncertain until systematic experiments are performed. Effects of processing variations (such as deposition parameters and annealing conditions) on interfacial bonding and long-term stability also remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cu substrate samples. One set receives the CuMoTaWV HEA coating by sputtering followed by annealing at 300 °C; the control set remains uncoated. Subject both sets to reciprocating wear tests at room temperature and 300 °C under a consistent sliding load. Conduct adhesion tests (e.g., scratch tests) and measure the wear volume and coefficient of friction.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during wear testing
Wear rate (volume loss measured via profilometry)
Critical load for coating failure in scratch tests
Surface morphology and interfacial integrity by SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-coated Cu matrix does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and improved adhesion (e.g., lower coefficient of friction and higher critical load in scratch test) compared to the uncoated Cu matrix, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
